disease.name: Kidney Stones
disease.icd_10_code: N20-N23 (Calculus of kidney and ureter); N20.0 (Calculus of kidney); N20.1 (Calculus of ureter); N20.2 (Calculus of kidney with calculus of ureter); N21 (Calculus of lower urinary tract); N23 (Unspecified renal colic)

overview.description: Kidney stones (nephrolithiasis) are hard, crystalline mineral and salt deposits that form within the kidneys or elsewhere in the urinary tract when the urine becomes supersaturated with stone-forming substances. They range from the size of a grain of sand to a golf ball and may remain asymptomatic for years or suddenly cause excruciating flank pain (renal colic) — often described as one of the most severe pains known to medicine — when they begin to move through the ureter. Kidney stones are among the most common urological disorders globally, with a lifetime prevalence of 10-15% in Western populations, and carry a high recurrence rate of approximately 50% within 5 years without preventive measures.
overview.prevalence: Lifetime risk: 10-15% in Western populations; 12% in the USA; 6-10% in India; affects approximately 1 in 11 Americans; global prevalence increasing due to obesity, metabolic syndrome, climate change, and dietary changes.
overview.age_group: Most common in adults aged 20-60 years; peak incidence 40-60 years; men affected 2-3 times more than women before age 50; female incidence rising; paediatric incidence increasing.
overview.sex_ratio: Men affected 2-3 times more than women overall; women increasingly affected; calcium phosphate and struvite stones more common in women; uric acid and cystine stones more common in men.
overview.recurrence_rate: Without preventive treatment: 50% recurrence within 5 years; 80% within 10 years. With targeted dietary and medical prevention: recurrence reduced by 50-80%.
overview.note: A stone-forming tendency is lifelong — while individual stones can be passed or removed, the underlying metabolic predisposition requires ongoing management

anatomy_and_pathophysiology.normal_urine_composition: Urine contains calcium, oxalate, phosphate, uric acid, citrate, magnesium, and other ions. In normal urine, inhibitors (citrate, Tamm-Horsfall protein, nephrocalcin, osteopontin) and adequate urine volume prevent crystal aggregation.

stone_formation_mechanism.step_1_supersaturation: When urine becomes supersaturated with stone-forming substances — from high dietary intake, low fluid intake, or metabolic disorders — dissolved ions exceed their solubility product (Ksp) and crystals begin to form
stone_formation_mechanism.step_2_nucleation: Crystal nuclei form either spontaneously (homogeneous nucleation) or on a surface like existing crystal, renal papillary epithelium, or Randall's plaques (calcium phosphate deposits on renal papillary tips — the starting point for calcium oxalate stones)
stone_formation_mechanism.step_3_growth_and_aggregation: Crystal nuclei grow and aggregate — this growth is favoured by high supersaturation and inhibited by urinary citrate, magnesium, and Tamm-Horsfall protein
stone_formation_mechanism.step_4_stone_formation: Crystals anchor to urothelium (Randall's plaque theory for calcium stones) or accumulate in collecting tubules, eventually forming a clinically significant stone
stone_formation_mechanism.ureteral_obstruction: When a stone enters the ureter, peristaltic contractions cause ureteral spasm and obstruction. Ureteral obstruction raises intraluminal pressure, causing ipsilateral hydronephrosis and activating prostaglandin synthesis — the primary mediator of renal colic pain

anatomy_and_pathophysiology.anatomical_narrowings: Three natural narrowings where stones tend to lodge: (1) Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ); (2) Crossing of the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim; (3) Ureterovesical junction (UVJ — narrowest, most common site of impaction)
anatomy_and_pathophysiology.randalls_plaques: Calcium phosphate deposits at the tips of renal papillae — the initial anchoring site for calcium oxalate stone formation; found on renal papilla surface; prevalence correlates with stone-forming tendency

types.name: Calcium Oxalate Stones
types.prevalence: Most common — 70-80% of all kidney stones

subtypes.name: Calcium oxalate monohydrate (whewellite)
subtypes.description: Harder, more dense; associated with hyperoxaluria and low urine volume; brown/black colour

subtypes.name: Calcium oxalate dihydrate (weddellite)
subtypes.description: Slightly more friable; associated with hypercalciuria; light yellow/brown colour

types.radiology: Radiopaque on plain X-ray (KUB); clearly visible on CT
types.causes: Hypercalciuria (most common), hyperoxaluria, hypocitraturia, low urine volume, hyperuricosuria (promotes heterogeneous nucleation of calcium oxalate)
types.prevention: High fluid intake; normal calcium diet (1000-1200mg/day); low oxalate diet; low sodium diet; potassium citrate; thiazide diuretics for hypercalciuria; allopurinol for hyperuricosuria

types.name: Calcium Phosphate Stones
types.prevalence: 10-20% of all stones; often mixed with calcium oxalate

subtypes.name: Hydroxyapatite
subtypes.description: Most common calcium phosphate type; associated with renal tubular acidosis (RTA) and primary hyperparathyroidism

subtypes.name: Brushite (calcium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate)
subtypes.description: More soluble than hydroxyapatite; associated with hypercalciuria and high urine pH; harder to fragment with ESWL

types.causes: Hypercalciuria, renal tubular acidosis type 1 (distal RTA — alkaline urine pH consistently >6.0), primary hyperparathyroidism, medullary sponge kidney
types.prevention: Treat underlying hypercalciuria; acidify urine if RTA (difficult); thiazide diuretics for hypercalciuria; potassium citrate (carefully — can raise pH)

types.name: Uric Acid Stones
types.prevalence: 5-10% of all stones in Western countries; up to 25% in hot arid climates
types.radiology: RADIOLUCENT on plain X-ray (KUB) — NOT visible on plain X-ray; visible on CT (CT Hounsfield units 200-400); classic teaching point
types.causes: Hyperuricosuria (excess dietary purine, gout, myeloproliferative disorders, tumour lysis syndrome), persistently acidic urine pH <5.5 (most important factor — the stone forms in acid urine regardless of uric acid level), low urine volume, insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome (impairs renal ammonia production → acid urine)
associated_conditions: Metabolic syndrome / Type 2 diabetes (most common cause of uric acid stones in Western countries)
Myeloproliferative disorders (leukemia, lymphoma — massive urate turnover)
High purine diet (organ meats, shellfish, beer)
types.urine_ph: Form only when urine pH persistently <5.5; completely soluble at pH >7.0
types.unique_feature: CAN BE COMPLETELY DISSOLVED (chemolysis) by urine alkalinisation with potassium citrate — the ONLY common stone type amenable to medical dissolution
types.prevention: Potassium citrate (alkalinise urine to pH 6.0-6.5); high fluid intake; low purine diet; allopurinol for hyperuricosuria; febuxostat as alternative

types.name: Struvite Stones (Infection Stones / Triple Phosphate / Magnesium Ammonium Phosphate)
types.prevalence: 5-15% of all stones; account for majority of staghorn calculi
types.radiology: Radiopaque; can be very large; classic appearance: staghorn configuration filling renal pelvis and calyces
types.causes: ALWAYS associated with urinary tract infection by urease-producing bacteria. Urease splits urinary urea into ammonia (NH4+) and bicarbonate (CO3 2-) → strongly alkaline urine (pH >7.5) → precipitation of magnesium, ammonium, and phosphate crystals
urease_producing_bacteria: NOT Escherichia coli — E. coli does NOT produce urease
types.urine_ph: Require alkaline urine (pH >7.5) from urease activity
types.unique_features: Can grow rapidly to fill the entire renal collecting system (staghorn calculi); associated with persistent UTI and urosepsis; cause significant renal damage if untreated; recur unless all stone material completely removed
types.prevention: Complete stone removal (essential); long-term antibiotics (culture-guided); urease inhibitor (acetohydroxamic acid — limited use due to side effects); address underlying urological abnormality

types.name: Cystine Stones
types.prevalence: 1-3% of all stones in adults; up to 8% in children
types.radiology: Mildly radiopaque ('ground glass' appearance on plain X-ray); clearly visible on CT with characteristic Hounsfield units
types.causes: Cystinuria — autosomal recessive (SLC3A1 gene Type A; SLC7A9 gene Type B) defect in renal tubular and intestinal transport of cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine (COLA). Cystine is the least soluble of these amino acids — precipitates in urine. Strongly familial.
types.unique_features: Exclusively hereditary; presents in childhood or young adulthood; highly recurrent and resistant to treatment; can form large staghorn stones; urinary cystine >250 mg/g creatinine is diagnostic
types.diagnostic_test: Sodium nitroprusside (cyanide-nitroprusside) urine test — turns purple-pink; 24-hour urinary cystine quantification
types.urine_ph: Cystine solubility increases significantly at pH >7.5
types.prevention: Very high fluid intake (>3L/day, aiming for urine volume >3L); urine alkalinisation to pH 7.0-7.5 (potassium citrate or sodium bicarbonate); D-penicillamine (chelates cystine but high side effect profile); tiopronin (alpha-mercaptopropionylglycine — preferred agent; fewer side effects than D-penicillamine); captopril (modest chelating effect via thiol group)

types.name: Drug-Induced Stones
types.prevalence: 1-2% of all stones; increasing with use of specific medications

examples.note: Radiolucent; precipitates in urine; classic in HIV patients; specific solubility issue
Increases intestinal oxalate absorption → calcium oxalate stones
Increase urinary calcium; risk with vitamin D co-supplementation
Converted to oxalate — increases urinary oxalate

types.management: Identify and stop causative drug where possible; high fluid intake; specific measures depending on drug type

types.name: Staghorn Calculi
types.description: Large stones that fill and partially or completely occupy the renal pelvis and calyces, resembling the shape of a stag's antlers. Most commonly composed of struvite, but can be calcium oxalate, uric acid, or mixed composition.
types.prevalence: Approximately 15% of all stones require active surgical intervention; more common in women (associated with urease-positive UTI)
types.classification: Complete staghorn: fills entire collecting system; Partial staghorn: fills part of collecting system
types.management: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is treatment of choice; multiple procedures often needed; antibiotic-guided therapy for struvite; complete stone clearance essential
types.prognosis: Untreated staghorn calculi eventually cause renal cortical scarring, pyelonephritis, obstructive nephropathy, and end-stage renal disease (ESRD)

severity_levels.name: Asymptomatic / Incidental Stone
severity_levels.description: Stone discovered incidentally on imaging performed for another reason; no symptoms of renal colic
severity_levels.stone_size: Usually <5mm; any size if in non-obstructing position
severity_levels.functional_impact: None currently; risk of future symptomatic episode
severity_levels.management: Conservative management; dietary and fluid modification; serial imaging every 12-24 months; metabolic evaluation; plan active treatment if stone grows or becomes symptomatic

severity_levels.name: Mild — Passing Stone (Renal Colic, Stone Likely to Pass Spontaneously)
severity_levels.description: Symptomatic renal colic with stone expected to pass with conservative management
severity_levels.stone_size: ≤5mm in ureter (80-90% spontaneous passage rate within 4 weeks); ≤10mm with medical expulsive therapy
severity_levels.pain: Moderate to severe flank pain — manageable with oral analgesics
severity_levels.functional_impact: Discomfort; may need time off work temporarily
severity_levels.management: Oral NSAIDs (first-line analgesics); anti-emetics; high fluid intake; medical expulsive therapy (alpha-blocker tamsulosin); strainer to catch stone for analysis; outpatient follow-up

severity_levels.name: Moderate — Persistent Stone Requiring Intervention
severity_levels.description: Stone that has failed to pass spontaneously after 4-6 weeks, or stone unlikely to pass based on size/location, causing ongoing symptoms
severity_levels.pain: Recurrent or persistent severe flank pain requiring opioid analgesia or repeated ED visits
severity_levels.functional_impact: Significant — inability to work; repeated hospital attendance
severity_levels.management: Urological referral; ESWL (extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy) for 5-20mm stones; ureteroscopy (URS) with laser lithotripsy for ureteric stones; adequate analgesia; infection screen

severity_levels.name: Severe — Obstructed Kidney with Complications
severity_levels.description: Stone causing significant ureteral/ureteropelvic junction obstruction with hydronephrosis, risk of renal function loss, or concurrent infection
severity_levels.stone_size: >10mm; any size in single kidney; any size with infection
severity_levels.pain: Severe, unrelenting pain requiring IV analgesia
severity_levels.functional_impact: Hospitalisation required; risk of renal function loss
severity_levels.management: Hospitalisation; IV analgesia; IV antibiotics if infection; urgent ureteral stent insertion (JJ stent) or nephrostomy tube to relieve obstruction; definitive stone removal procedure (PCNL, URS) after stabilisation

severity_levels.name: Critical — Infected Obstructed System (Obstructive Uropathy with Urosepsis)
severity_levels.description: The most dangerous kidney stone complication — obstructed kidney with concurrent UTI causing sepsis. The combination of obstruction AND infection creates a closed pus-filled system that rapidly leads to urosepsis and septic shock. This is a UROLOGICAL EMERGENCY with significant mortality.
severity_levels.clinical_features: High fever (>38.5°C) or hypothermia + loin pain + features of SIRS/sepsis (tachycardia, hypotension, confusion) in the context of known or suspected ureteral stone
severity_levels.management: IMMEDIATE ICU-level care; urgent IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone + metronidazole); URGENT ureteral decompression — JJ stent under spinal anaesthesia or ultrasound-guided nephrostomy tube (do NOT do definitive stone removal in infected field); IV fluid resuscitation; vasopressors if septic shock; definitive stone removal only after infection cleared
severity_levels.mortality: Septic shock from obstructed infected kidney: 20-40% without urgent drainage

primary_risk_factors.description: The SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT modifiable risk factor for all stone types. Insufficient fluid intake produces concentrated urine with high supersaturation of stone-forming ions. Target urine output >2.0-2.5L/day. Each 0.5L increase in daily urine output reduces stone recurrence risk by 50%.
primary_risk_factors.prevalence: Present in virtually all stone formers as a contributing factor

primary_risk_factors.description: Urinary calcium >250mg/day (women) or >300mg/day (men) is the most common metabolic abnormality in calcium stone formers — present in 30-60%. Subtypes: absorptive (increased intestinal calcium absorption — most common), renal (decreased tubular calcium reabsorption), and resorptive (excessive bone resorption as in primary hyperparathyroidism).
primary_risk_factors.causes: Primary hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, immobilisation, idiopathic hypercalciuria (genetic), high sodium diet (reduces tubular reabsorption of calcium), sarcoidosis

primary_risk_factors.description: Urinary oxalate >45mg/day (women) or >40mg/day (men). Even a moderate increase in urinary oxalate dramatically increases calcium oxalate stone risk (oxalate's contribution to supersaturation is far greater than calcium).
primary_risk_factors.causes: Dietary (excess spinach, nuts, chocolate, tea, beets — exogenous); enteric hyperoxaluria from fat malabsorption (IBD, Crohn's, bariatric surgery, short bowel syndrome — unabsorbed fatty acids bind calcium in gut, leaving oxalate free for absorption); primary hyperoxaluria types I and II (genetic — rare, severe, often causes kidney failure)

primary_risk_factors.description: Urinary citrate <320mg/day is a major risk factor — citrate is the most important naturally occurring inhibitor of calcium stone formation (chelates calcium in urine, reducing free ionic calcium available for crystallisation; directly inhibits crystal nucleation and growth).
primary_risk_factors.causes: Distal renal tubular acidosis (type 1 RTA), chronic diarrhoea, inflammatory bowel disease, high protein diet (metabolic acidosis reduces citrate excretion), potassium deficiency, thiazide diuretics (can cause hypocitraturia), UTI

primary_risk_factors.description: Urinary uric acid >600-750mg/day in women or >800mg/day in men. Promotes heterogeneous nucleation of calcium oxalate crystals (uric acid crystals provide a template for calcium oxalate crystal growth). Also forms uric acid stones in persistently acid urine.
primary_risk_factors.causes: High purine diet (red meat, organ meats, shellfish, beer), gout, metabolic syndrome, myeloproliferative disorders

primary_risk_factors.description: Essential for uric acid stone formation — uric acid is insoluble at pH <5.5. Associated with metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, gout, and chronic diarrhoea/ileostomy (bicarbonate loss). Low urine pH also promotes brushite stone dissolution but calcium oxalate formation is pH-independent.

Promotes calcium phosphate and struvite stone formation. Associated with distal RTA (type 1), urinary tract infection with urease-producing organisms, vegetarian diet, and excessive alkali supplementation.

Excess parathyroid hormone (PTH) causes: hypercalcaemia (elevated serum calcium); hypercalciuria (excess calcium filtered by kidney); hypophosphataemia; elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (increases intestinal calcium absorption). Present in 3-8% of calcium stone formers. Often diagnosed incidentally from stone metabolic workup.
primary_risk_factors.diagnosis: Elevated PTH with elevated serum calcium; confirm with repeat measurements
primary_risk_factors.treatment: Parathyroidectomy (curative) — completely eliminates the parathyroid-mediated stone risk

dietary_risk_factors: High animal protein diet — increases urinary calcium, oxalate, and uric acid; decreases urinary citrate and pH; most powerful dietary stone-promoter
High sodium diet — increases urinary calcium (every 100mmol sodium excretion = 25mg calcium excretion reduction in tubular reabsorption)
High fructose / refined sugar diet — increases urinary calcium, oxalate, and uric acid; promotes metabolic syndrome and acid urine
High oxalate diet — spinach, almonds, cashews, peanuts, chocolate, beets, wheat bran, tea, rhubarb, sweet potato
Low calcium diet — paradoxically INCREASES stone risk because dietary calcium normally binds intestinal oxalate preventing its absorption; low dietary calcium allows more oxalate absorption
Excessive calcium supplements (especially without meals) — increase urinary calcium without the protective effect of binding intestinal oxalate
High vitamin C supplement intake (>1g/day) — converted to oxalate in the body
Low fluid intake — most important risk factor
High caffeine intake — diuretic effect; may increase urinary calcium
genetic_and_hereditary_factors: Family history of kidney stones — first-degree relatives have 2.5x higher risk
Cystinuria — autosomal recessive SLC3A1 / SLC7A9 mutations
Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (AGXT gene mutation) and type 2 (GRHPR gene) — rare, severe
Distal renal tubular acidosis (type 1 RTA) — hereditary forms
Dent's disease (CLCN5 mutation) — X-linked hypercalciuric nephrolithiasis
Hyperoxaluria associated with AGXT2 and HOGA1 variants
anatomical_and_structural_factors: Horseshoe kidney — impaired drainage; stone formation in lower moiety calyces
Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction — urinary stasis promotes stone formation
Medullary sponge kidney (tubular ectasia) — impaired drainage in collecting tubules; calcium phosphate stones
Vesicoureteral reflux — stasis and recurrent infection
Bladder outlet obstruction / benign prostatic hyperplasia
Single kidney — higher risk consequences; requires aggressive prevention
medical_conditions_and_medications: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease) — enteric hyperoxaluria from fat malabsorption; hypocitraturia from bicarbonate loss
Bariatric surgery (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass) — dramatically increases calcium oxalate stone risk from enteric hyperoxaluria
Gout — hyperuricaemia and hyperuricosuria → uric acid stones
Metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes — insulin resistance impairs renal ammoniagenesis → acid urine → uric acid stones
Sarcoidosis — excess vitamin D production → hypercalciuria
Renal tubular acidosis (type 1 distal) — alkaline urine, hypocitraturia → calcium phosphate/oxalate stones
Immobilisation (fractures, spinal cord injury, prolonged bed rest) — bone resorption → hypercalciuria

Medications: furosemide (hypercalciuria), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (topiramate, acetazolamide — alkaline urine → calcium phosphate), calcium antacids, vitamin D excess, orlistat, protease inhibitors

primary_symptoms.name: Renal Colic — Severe Flank Pain
primary_symptoms.description: The hallmark symptom — sudden, severe, excruciating, colicky (wave-like) pain originating in the flank (loin) region between the last rib and the hip, caused by ureteral spasm and distension from obstruction. Unlike peritoneal pain, patients cannot find a comfortable position and typically writhe in agony. Often described as 10/10 severity — 'worse than childbirth' by many women. Pain radiates characteristically depending on stone location: upper ureter → flank + upper abdomen; mid-ureter → flank + abdomen + groin; lower ureter → flank + groin + ipsilateral testis or labia; UVJ → urinary urgency and frequency mimicking cystitis. Onset typically sudden, at rest or during physical activity.
primary_symptoms.onset: Sudden; rapidly escalating; may persist continuously or in severe waves (colic)
primary_symptoms.pain_pattern: Colicky (comes in severe waves) with background constant pain; does NOT relieve with position change — distinguishes from musculoskeletal pain

primary_symptoms.name: Haematuria (Blood in Urine)
primary_symptoms.description: Blood in urine — present in 85-90% of cases of acute renal colic. Can be macroscopic (visible pink, red, or brown urine — gross haematuria) or microscopic (only detectable on dipstick or microscopy). Caused by stone trauma to the urothelium. Absence of haematuria does NOT exclude stone — present in only 85-90% of cases.
primary_symptoms.note: Painless macroscopic haematuria (blood without pain) is NOT typical of kidney stones and requires urgent investigation for bladder cancer or other serious pathology

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea and Vomiting
primary_symptoms.description: Severe nausea and vomiting affect 50-60% of patients with acute renal colic — from visceral pain activation (vagal response) and renal pelvic distension triggering the celio-mesenteric plexus. Vomiting prevents adequate oral analgesia and fluid intake. Anti-emetics are an essential component of renal colic management.

primary_symptoms.name: Urinary Urgency and Frequency
primary_symptoms.description: Sudden urge to urinate and increased urination frequency — characteristic when a stone is located in the distal ureter close to the bladder (ureterovesical junction) or within the bladder. The stone irritates the trigone and ureterovesical junction, causing irritative bladder symptoms that closely mimic urinary tract infection. Dysuria (painful urination) also common with distal ureteric stones.
primary_symptoms.onset: As stone moves distally towards the bladder

primary_symptoms.name: Costovertebral Angle (CVA) Tenderness
primary_symptoms.description: Tenderness on percussion or deep palpation at the costovertebral angle — the angle between the last rib and the spine on the affected side. This is the clinical correlate of ipsilateral hydronephrosis and renal pelvic distension. Very common physical examination finding in acute renal colic — helps lateralise the obstructed side. Bilateral tenderness should prompt investigation of bilateral obstruction or other causes.
primary_symptoms.onset: During acute episode; may persist with chronic obstruction

primary_symptoms.name: Oliguria or Reduced Urine Output
primary_symptoms.description: Decreased urine output from the obstructed kidney. In the case of a single kidney or bilateral obstruction, total urine output may decrease significantly — a medical emergency. In patients with two functioning kidneys, the contralateral kidney compensates and total urine output may be maintained.
primary_symptoms.severity: Moderate to Severe — emergency if bilateral or single kidney

secondary_symptoms: Fever and chills — DANGER SIGN — suggests concurrent urinary tract infection with obstruction (obstructed infected kidney = urological emergency)
Restlessness and inability to find a comfortable position (classic renal colic behaviour) — contrasts with peritonitis where patients lie still
Sweating and pallor from severe pain
Abdominal distension and ileus from retroperitoneal pain and vagal stimulation
Abdominal tenderness (ipsilateral lower quadrant) — from distal ureteric stone irritating adjacent bowel
Referred testicular or labial pain (from lower ureteric stones — genitofemoral nerve distribution)
Decreased appetite and inability to eat during pain episodes
Fatigue and lethargy (chronic obstruction or recurrent episodes)
Flank fullness or dull ache (hydronephrosis from partial obstruction — chronic)
warning_signs_of_attack: Fever >38°C with unilateral flank pain and stone — OBSTRUCTED INFECTED KIDNEY — UROLOGICAL EMERGENCY — do not delay drainage
Severe pain uncontrolled by oral analgesics requiring IV morphine repeatedly
Signs of sepsis: tachycardia, hypotension, confusion with flank pain — septic shock from urosepsis
Complete inability to pass urine (anuria) — bilateral obstruction or single kidney obstruction — emergency
Stone in a single functioning kidney — obstruction of the only kidney is a medical emergency
Severe vomiting preventing any oral intake including analgesia and fluids
symptoms_in_children: Flank or abdominal pain — may be less specifically localised than in adults; colicky abdominal pain common presenting feature
Haematuria (visible or microscopic) — often the presenting symptom in children
Recurrent UTI in children — especially in girls — screen for underlying stone disease
Failure to thrive or growth retardation in infants with chronic renal obstruction
Urinary frequency and dysuria from distal ureteric stones
Vomiting and refusal to eat during colic episodes
Cystinuria in children: typically presents with first stone in childhood or adolescence
atypical_presentations: Asymptomatic hydronephrosis — partial UPJ obstruction from stone may be painless if gradual
Staghorn calculi — can be surprisingly asymptomatic despite massive stone burden; discovered incidentally
Pure haematuria without pain — uric acid stone or very small passing stone
Recurrent UTI — underlying struvite stone or structural abnormality
Renal failure — bilateral hydronephrosis from bilateral stones or bilateral obstruction

medical_history: Detailed pain history: onset, location (flank vs abdominal vs groin), character (colicky, constant), radiation pattern, severity (VAS), aggravating/relieving factors
Urinary symptoms: haematuria (macroscopic or microscopic), urinary frequency, urgency, dysuria, oliguria
Systemic symptoms: fever, chills, nausea, vomiting
Prior kidney stone history: number of stones, stone composition if analysed, prior procedures, recurrence pattern
Family history of kidney stones, gout, renal disease, hereditary conditions (cystinuria, hyperoxaluria)
Dietary history: fluid intake (daily urine output estimate), animal protein, sodium, oxalate-rich foods, calcium supplements, vitamin C supplements, caffeine
Medication history: calcium supplements, vitamin D, topiramate (raises urine pH → calcium phosphate), furosemide, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, protease inhibitors, orlistat
Medical history: gout, IBD, Crohn's disease, bariatric surgery, primary hyperparathyroidism, metabolic syndrome, diabetes, recurrent UTI, anatomical urinary tract abnormalities
Occupation and climate: hot, dry environment; outdoor worker; inadequate fluid intake
physical_examination: Vital signs: temperature (fever = infected stone — emergency), heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, SpO2
General appearance: patient in severe distress, writhing, unable to find comfortable position (classic renal colic); sweating; pale
Abdominal examination: inspection (distension, visible pulsation), auscultation (bowel sounds), percussion (tenderness), palpation (ipsilateral lower quadrant tenderness from distal ureteric stone)
Costovertebral angle (CVA) percussion: brisk, firm percussion at costovertebral angle on affected side — positive if produces sharp pain (Murphy's kidney punch); localises obstructed side
Flank fullness: visible or palpable flank mass in severe hydronephrosis

Genital examination in men: rule out epididymo-orchitis (testicular tenderness with scrotal erythema — mimics referred pain from ureteric stone); testicular torsion (twisting) must be excluded in young men with scrotal pain
Rectal examination in women: cervical motion tenderness (PID), adnexal masses (ovarian pathology) — exclude gynaecological causes
Hydration status: assessment in patients with vomiting
Neurological examination: exclude spinal pathology mimicking renal colic (disc prolapse with radiculopathy)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Non-Contrast CT KUB (CT Urogram / CT Stone Protocol)
diagnostic_tests.description: Gold standard investigation for suspected kidney stones — detects virtually all stone types regardless of composition (including radiolucent uric acid stones which are invisible on plain X-ray). Single CT KUB takes <5 minutes. Provides stone size, location, density (Hounsfield units — predicts composition and fragility), skin-to-stone distance (for ESWL planning), degree of hydronephrosis, perinephric stranding (inflammation), and alternative diagnoses.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm stone diagnosis; characterise stone size, location, and composition; assess degree of obstruction; exclude alternative diagnoses (appendicitis, ovarian pathology, aortic aneurysm)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Stone density: calcium oxalate monohydrate >800 HU; uric acid 200-400 HU; brushite >1200 HU; stone size in mm; degree of hydronephrosis (none, mild, moderate, severe); presence of perinephric fat stranding
diagnostic_tests.sensitivity: >95% sensitivity and specificity for stones ≥3mm; approaches 100% for clinically significant stones
diagnostic_tests.radiation: Low-dose CT protocols available; radiation dose ~1-3 mSv (standard abdominal CT 8-10 mSv); use low-dose protocol for young patients and those requiring repeated imaging

diagnostic_tests.description: First-line imaging in specific situations: pregnancy (avoids radiation), children (paediatric dose concern), known stone formers with typical recurrent colic (confirm hydronephrosis rather than new stone), and when CT unavailable. Detects hydronephrosis reliably but misses many smaller ureteric stones. Cannot directly visualise mid-ureteric stones in most cases.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect hydronephrosis and kidney stones; monitor stone in situ; follow-up imaging; safe in pregnancy and children; assess for complications
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Degree of hydronephrosis (mild: <1cm pelvic dilatation; moderate: 1-2cm; severe: >2cm); stone visible as echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadow
diagnostic_tests.sensitivity: 45-60% for ureteric stones; 90% for renal stones and hydronephrosis; significantly inferior to CT for stone detection
diagnostic_tests.advantages: No radiation; bedside available; safe in pregnancy; real-time

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Plain Abdominal X-Ray (KUB — Kidneys, Ureters, Bladder)
diagnostic_tests.description: Simple, readily available, low-radiation X-ray of the abdomen showing the urinary tract. Detects radiopaque stones (calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, struvite). Misses radiolucent stones (uric acid, cystine, drug-induced), small stones, and stones overlying bony structures.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect radiopaque stones; monitor stone clearance after treatment; assess response to ESWL (stone fragmentation); quick screening
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Radiopaque stones: calcium oxalate and phosphate highly radiopaque; struvite moderately radiopaque. Radiolucent: uric acid NOT visible; cystine mildly radiopaque
diagnostic_tests.sensitivity: 50-60% for renal stones; better for larger calcified stones; inferior to CT for all stone types
diagnostic_tests.uses: Still useful for monitoring known radiopaque stones and post-treatment stone burden assessment

diagnostic_tests.description: IV contrast injected and sequential X-rays show the contrast filling the collecting system, delineating anatomy and obstruction (delayed or absent excretion from obstructed kidney). Largely replaced by CT for stone diagnosis but still used for detailed anatomical assessment pre-operatively.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess collecting system anatomy; detect obstruction and degree of hydronephrosis; delineate site of obstruction; pre-operative planning
diagnostic_tests.note: Requires normal renal function (contrast nephropathy risk); requires IV iodine contrast (allergy risk); largely superseded by CT for acute stone diagnosis

diagnostic_tests.description: Essential first-line test. Dipstick detects haematuria (blood — present in 85% of renal colic), pyuria/nitrites (UTI — critical to detect in stone patient), pH. Microscopy identifies red blood cells, white blood cells, bacteria, and importantly CRYSTALS — crystal type strongly suggests stone composition: calcium oxalate (dumbbell/envelope/needle shape), uric acid (diamond/barrel shape), cystine (hexagonal flat plates — pathognomonic), struvite (coffin-lid/prism shape).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect haematuria (supports stone diagnosis); detect UTI (changes management — emergency if with obstruction); assess urine pH (acid: uric acid stones; alkaline: phosphate/struvite stones); crystal identification
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Haematuria: ≥3 RBCs/hpf. pH <5.5: uric acid stone risk. pH >7.5 with ammonia smell: struvite (infection stone). Cystine crystals (hexagonal flat): diagnostic of cystinuria

diagnostic_tests.description: Mandatory in ALL patients with kidney stones — UTI with obstruction is a life-threatening emergency. Culture identifies organism and antibiotic sensitivity for: treatment of concurrent infection, guidance for perioperative antibiotics before stone intervention, and identification of urease-producing organisms (struvite stone aetiology).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect concurrent UTI; guide antibiotic therapy before stone intervention; identify urease-producing bacteria (struvite aetiology); MANDATORY before any surgical stone procedure
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Significant bacteriuria: >10^5 CFU/mL. Urease-positive bacteria (Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas) in stone patient strongly suggests struvite stones

diagnostic_tests.description: Comprehensive metabolic screen for all stone formers. Serum calcium (hyperparathyroidism), phosphate, uric acid, electrolytes (RTA), bicarbonate (metabolic acidosis/RTA), renal function (creatinine/eGFR — degree of obstruction/CKD).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect primary hyperparathyroidism (elevated calcium); detect hyperuricaemia (uric acid stones/gout); assess renal function (eGFR — critically important for treatment planning); detect metabolic acidosis (RTA type 1); electrolyte abnormalities
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Serum calcium >2.6 mmol/L: screen for primary hyperparathyroidism (measure PTH); Uric acid >420 µmol/L (men) or >360 µmol/L (women): hyperuricaemia; Creatinine + eGFR: baseline renal function

diagnostic_tests.description: Elevated PTH in the context of elevated serum calcium = primary hyperparathyroidism (surgically curable cause of calcium stones). 25-OH vitamin D should be measured — vitamin D deficiency is common and should NOT be aggressively supplemented in stone formers without first measuring urinary calcium response.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose primary hyperparathyroidism (3-8% of calcium stone formers); assess vitamin D status
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: PTH elevated + serum calcium elevated = primary hyperparathyroidism; PTH elevated + normal serum calcium = secondary hyperparathyroidism (vitamin D deficiency, CKD)

diagnostic_tests.type: Urine — Biochemical (Gold Standard for Prevention Planning)
diagnostic_tests.description: The most important investigation for designing targeted stone prevention therapy. Patient collects ALL urine for a complete 24-hour period (including first morning void the next day). Measures urinary calcium, oxalate, uric acid, citrate, phosphate, creatinine (adequacy check), pH, volume, and sodium. At least 2 collections recommended. Performed during normal diet AND after dietary modification.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: COMPREHENSIVE metabolic evaluation to identify ALL urinary risk factors; direct targeted preventive therapy (e.g., identify if thiazide diuretic, potassium citrate, or allopurinol is needed); monitor response to treatment

parameters.citrate: Normal >320mg/day. Low = hypocitraturia — most important inhibitor deficiency
parameters.pH: Measured in collected urine; <5.5 = uric acid risk; >7.0 = calcium phosphate or struvite risk
parameters.creatinine: Validates completeness of collection: 15-20mg/kg/day men, 10-15mg/kg/day women

diagnostic_tests.note: Indicated for all recurrent stone formers, first-time stone formers with risk factors (family history, metabolic conditions, solitary kidney), and children with any stone. Performed 6-8 weeks after acute episode.

diagnostic_tests.description: Every passed or retrieved stone should be sent for compositional analysis — it is the single most informative investigation for directing targeted stone prevention therapy. Methods: X-ray diffraction (most accurate — identifies crystal structure), infrared spectrophotometry, or chemical analysis. The stone type directly dictates dietary and pharmacological prevention strategy.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Definitively identify stone composition; direct targeted prevention therapy; may reveal unexpected rare types (cystine, drug-induced, 2,8-dihydroxyadenine); essential for every retrievable stone
diagnostic_tests.instructions: Strain all urine; collect any passed stone fragments; preserve in dry container (NOT in water which dissolves some components); send for laboratory analysis

diagnostic_tests.description: Screening test for cystinuria. Fresh urine sample + sodium nitroprusside + sodium cyanide — turns purple-pink if cystine present. Positive result indicates significant cystinuria. Confirmatory test: 24-hour urine cystine quantification (>250mg/g creatinine is diagnostic).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for cystinuria in young stone formers, recurrent stone formers, and children with stones; positive test changes prevention strategy completely

diagnostic_tests.description: Leukocytosis with neutrophilia and elevated CRP indicate infection — critical to detect in any stone patient. High WBC + elevated CRP with flank pain in a known or suspected stone patient = infected obstructed kidney until proven otherwise (emergency decompression required).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect systemic infection (obstructed infected kidney); screen for sepsis; baseline before intervention
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: WBC >12,000/µL + CRP >50mg/L in stone patient with fever: treat as obstructed infected kidney — emergency ureteral drainage

diagnostic_tests.description: Direct endoscopic visualisation of the ureter and renal collecting system using a flexible ureteroscope. Allows direct stone visualisation, biopsy of suspicious lesions, and simultaneous treatment. Primarily therapeutic but can be diagnostic when CT is inconclusive.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Direct stone visualisation and treatment; diagnosis of urothelial lesions mimicking stone symptoms (transitional cell carcinoma — TCC); biopsy suspicious lesions

medicines.note: Kidney stone management involves: (1) ACUTE treatment — pain relief, anti-emetics, and medical expulsive therapy to facilitate stone passage; (2) PROCEDURAL treatment — interventional removal of larger or non-passing stones; (3) PREVENTIVE medical therapy — targeted pharmacological treatment to correct underlying metabolic abnormalities and prevent recurrence. All medications must be prescribed by a licensed urologist or physician.
treatment_goals: Acute: Immediate pain relief; treat associated infection; facilitate stone passage
Subacute: Determine need for intervention vs conservative management based on stone size, location, symptoms, and presence of complications
Long-term: Prevent recurrence through dietary modification and targeted pharmacological prevention

categories.purpose: Provide immediate, effective pain relief for acute renal colic — one of the most severe pain syndromes in medicine. NSAIDs are the preferred first-line analgesics because they block prostaglandin synthesis (the mediator of renal colic pain) AND reduce ureteral peristalsis. Opioids are second-line or rescue analgesia.
categories.note: Give analgesics IMMEDIATELY and in adequate doses — renal colic is a pain emergency; pain control should not be delayed

medicines.name: Diclofenac Sodium
medicines.form: IM/IV Injection, Rectal suppository (100mg), Oral tablet
medicines.dosage: IM: 75mg single dose (may repeat once after 30 min; max 150mg/day); Rectal: 100mg suppository; Oral: 50mg three times daily; IV: 75mg over 30 min
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE analgesic for acute renal colic; IM or rectal route preferred for rapid onset and when vomiting prevents oral intake. Evidence: NSAIDs superior to opioids for renal colic (better pain control + fewer side effects)
medicines.mechanism: COX-1/COX-2 inhibitor; reduces prostaglandin synthesis — decreases ureteral smooth muscle spasm AND reduces renal pelvic pressure from collecting system contraction
side_effects: Renal impairment (avoid in significant renal failure — eGFR <30)
medicines.evidence: Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses confirm: diclofenac/ketorolac NSAIDs provide equal or superior pain relief to opioids for renal colic with fewer adverse effects

medicines.name: Ketorolac Tromethamine
medicines.dosage: 30mg IV or IM initially; 15-30mg every 6 hours (max 5 days; max 90mg/day IV; 120mg/day IM)
medicines.use_case: IV NSAID for acute renal colic when IV access established (emergency department); most commonly used IV NSAID; rapid onset within minutes IV

medicines.name: Indomethacin
medicines.dosage: Rectal: 100mg suppository; can repeat after 4 hours; Oral: 25-50mg three times daily
medicines.use_case: Highly effective rectal NSAID for renal colic when IV access not available or when vomiting prevents oral intake; rectal route has rapid absorption comparable to IV
medicines.note: Rectal indomethacin provides near-IV speed of onset and very effective renal colic control

medicines.name: Morphine Sulfate
medicines.dosage: IV: 0.1mg/kg titrated; 2-5mg IV boluses; IM: 10mg; PCA (patient-controlled analgesia) for severe/refractory pain
medicines.use_case: Second-line or combination therapy for renal colic when NSAIDs alone are insufficient; useful when NSAIDs contraindicated; IV morphine + IV NSAID combination provides best pain control
side_effects: Nausea and vomiting (may worsen stone-related vomiting — give antiemetic)
medicines.note: Opioids may increase smooth muscle spasm — may not directly reduce ureteral spasm unlike NSAIDs

medicines.name: Tramadol
medicines.dosage: 50-100mg IV/IM; 50-100mg orally
medicines.use_case: Moderate pain relief; alternative to morphine for moderate renal colic

medicines.name: Paracetamol / Acetaminophen (IV)
medicines.dosage: 1000mg IV over 15 minutes every 6 hours
medicines.use_case: Adjunct analgesic alongside NSAIDs; useful when NSAIDs contraindicated (renal impairment, NSAID allergy); multimodal analgesia; IV formulation provides rapid onset
medicines.note: Inferior to NSAIDs for renal colic as monotherapy but valuable as part of multimodal regimen

medicines.name: Hyoscine Butylbromide (Buscopan)
medicines.dosage: 20mg IV or IM
medicines.use_case: Antispasmodic — reduces ureteral smooth muscle spasm; adjunct to NSAIDs; most useful for colicky component of pain; widely used in India for renal colic
medicines.mechanism: Anticholinergic antispasmodic; reduces smooth muscle spasm in ureter and GI tract

categories.category_name: Medical Expulsive Therapy (MET) — Alpha-1 Adrenergic Blockers
categories.purpose: Facilitate spontaneous passage of ureteric stones by relaxing ureteral smooth muscle and reducing ureteral spasm. Most effective for distal ureteric stones 4-10mm. Reduces time to stone passage and need for analgesia. EAU guideline-recommended.
categories.evidence: Meta-analyses confirm: alpha-blockers increase stone passage rate by 29-44% for stones 5-10mm; reduce time to passage by ~4 days. Most benefit for 5-10mm distal ureteral stones.
categories.duration: Continue for up to 4 weeks while stone attempts spontaneous passage; if no passage by 4-6 weeks — refer for urological intervention

medicines.name: Tamsulosin
medicines.dosage: 0.4mg once daily (taken 30 minutes after same meal each day); continue until stone passes or for maximum 4 weeks
medicines.use_case: MOST COMMONLY USED and recommended MET agent for ureteric stones 4-10mm; reduces ureteral spasm; increases stone passage rate; also reduces analgesic requirements; particularly effective for distal ureteric stones
medicines.mechanism: Highly selective alpha-1A/1D adrenergic receptor antagonist; relaxes smooth muscle in distal ureter, ureterovesical junction (UVJ), and bladder neck; decreases ureteral peristaltic amplitude
side_effects: Orthostatic hypotension and dizziness (most common — advise rising slowly, especially first few days)
Floppy iris syndrome (intraoperative — inform ophthalmologist if cataract surgery planned)
medicines.note: Most evidence for tamsulosin; uroselective so fewer systemic side effects than non-selective alpha-blockers

medicines.name: Silodosin
medicines.dosage: 8mg once daily with evening meal
medicines.use_case: MET for ureteric stones; highly uroselective alpha-1A blocker — may be more effective for ureteral smooth muscle relaxation; growing evidence

medicines.name: Alfuzosin
medicines.dosage: 10mg once daily after meal
medicines.use_case: MET alternative; less uroselective than tamsulosin — equivalent MET efficacy; once-daily dosing

medicines.name: Nifedipine (Calcium Channel Blocker — MET)
medicines.dosage: 30-60mg once daily (SR/LA formulation)
medicines.use_case: Alternative MET when alpha-blockers contraindicated; calcium channel blockade relaxes ureteral smooth muscle; less evidence than alpha-blockers; still used particularly with anti-inflammatory corticosteroid combination
medicines.note: Less evidence than alpha-blockers; guidelines currently favour alpha-blockers; still used in practice

categories.category_name: Antiemetics — Nausea Management in Renal Colic
categories.purpose: Control nausea and vomiting to allow oral analgesics and hydration, and for patient comfort. Essential adjunct to analgesia in acute renal colic.

medicines.name: Ondansetron
medicines.form: IV/IM Injection, ODT tablet, Oral tablet
medicines.dosage: 4-8mg IV/orally every 8 hours; 8mg IV for acute severe nausea
medicines.use_case: First-line antiemetic for renal colic-associated nausea and vomiting; safe and effective; ODT useful when vomiting prevents swallowing tablets

medicines.name: Metoclopramide
medicines.dosage: 10mg IV/IM/orally every 8 hours
medicines.use_case: Antiemetic and prokinetic for renal colic nausea

categories.category_name: Urine Alkalinisation — Uric Acid Stone Dissolution and Prevention
categories.purpose: Alkalinise urine to pH 6.0-7.0 — at this pH uric acid becomes soluble (urate). This is the ONLY stone type that can be completely dissolved non-surgically with medications. Also used for cystine stones (solubility increases at pH >7.5) and calcium oxalate with hypocitraturia.
categories.target_urine_ph: Uric acid dissolution: pH 6.5-7.0; uric acid prevention: pH 6.0-6.5; cystine: pH 7.0-7.5

medicines.name: Potassium Citrate
medicines.form: Granule sachets, Modified release tablet, Oral solution
medicines.dosage: 20-30 mEq/day in 3-4 divided doses (dissolution); 30-60 mEq/day for active dissolution of uric acid stone; monitor urine pH twice daily
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE for uric acid stone prevention and dissolution; prevents calcium oxalate stones (increases urinary citrate — stone inhibitor); cystine stones (alkalinises urine); hypocitraturia (directly replaces urinary citrate deficiency); distal RTA
medicines.mechanism: Absorbed as potassium and citrate; citrate is metabolised to bicarbonate, alkalinising blood and urine; increases urinary citrate (direct stone inhibitor); raises urine pH
side_effects: GI upset, nausea, diarrhoea (take with food or after meals)
Hyperkalaemia (monitor K+ — caution with ACEi/ARBs, renal failure)
Take with large glass of water
medicines.monitoring: Urine pH (twice daily home monitoring); serum potassium and creatinine
contraindications: UTI with Proteus (alkalinising urine promotes struvite)
medicines.note: Most versatile and important urinary alkaliniser; replaces citrate deficiency while alkalinising urine

medicines.name: Sodium Bicarbonate
medicines.dosage: 1-2g (12-24 mmol) 2-3 times daily; adjust to urine pH target
medicines.use_case: Urine alkalinisation when potassium citrate not available or not tolerated; cheaper alternative; also useful in distal RTA
side_effects: Sodium load — may worsen hypertension or fluid retention
medicines.note: Less preferred than potassium citrate because sodium load may increase urinary calcium (each 100mmol sodium = 25mg extra urinary calcium)

medicines.name: Sodium Citrate / Citric Acid (Shohl's Solution / Cytra-2)
medicines.dosage: 10-30mL of solution 3-4 times daily with meals
medicines.use_case: Alkalinisation; used in distal RTA; alternative to potassium citrate in patients intolerant of the granule form
medicines.note: Contains sodium — same cardiovascular caution as sodium bicarbonate

categories.category_name: Xanthine Oxidase Inhibitors — Uric Acid Stone Prevention
categories.purpose: Reduce uric acid production by inhibiting xanthine oxidase — the enzyme that converts xanthine to uric acid. Lower serum and urinary uric acid levels. Used for: hyperuricosuria-induced calcium oxalate stones AND uric acid stones with documented hyperuricosuria.

medicines.name: Allopurinol
medicines.dosage: 100-300mg once daily; start low (100mg) and titrate; adjust dose based on serum uric acid and urine uric acid levels; dose-reduce in renal impairment
medicines.use_case: Uric acid stones with hyperuricosuria (>600mg/day); calcium oxalate stones with hyperuricosuria (uric acid promotes calcium oxalate nucleation); gout with kidney stones; adjunct to alkalinisation for uric acid stone prevention
medicines.mechanism: Inhibits xanthine oxidase, blocking conversion of hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid; reduces serum and urinary uric acid
side_effects: Skin rash (2-3% — rarely severe Stevens-Johnson; stop immediately)
Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (rare but potentially fatal — HLA-B*58:01 increases risk in Asian populations)
medicines.monitoring: Uric acid levels (target <6mg/dL); LFTs; renal function; CBC; HLA-B*58:01 screening in high-risk Asian patients

medicines.name: Febuxostat
medicines.dosage: 40-80mg once daily; reduce dose in hepatic impairment
medicines.use_case: Alternative to allopurinol for uric acid stone prevention; particularly useful when allopurinol not tolerated or contraindicated; can be used in mild-moderate CKD without dose adjustment
side_effects: FDA black box: increased cardiovascular death vs allopurinol in patients with cardiovascular disease (CARES trial) — avoid if established CVD
medicines.note: More potent urate-lowering per mg than allopurinol; does not require dose adjustment for renal function

categories.purpose: Reduce urinary calcium excretion in idiopathic hypercalciuria — the most common metabolic abnormality in calcium stone formers. Thiazides increase distal tubular calcium reabsorption by 30-50%, dramatically reducing urinary calcium.
categories.indication: Urinary calcium >250mg/day (women) or >300mg/day (men) on 24-hour urine collection; recurrent calcium stones with hypercalciuria

medicines.name: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ)
medicines.dosage: 12.5-50mg once daily; start 12.5-25mg
medicines.use_case: Hypercalciuric calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate stones; reduces urinary calcium by 30-50%; reduces stone recurrence by 50% in controlled trials
medicines.mechanism: Inhibits NaCl cotransporter (NCC) in distal tubule; reduces tubular sodium reabsorption → volume contraction → compensatory increase in proximal tubular calcium reabsorption → decreased urinary calcium
side_effects: Hypokalaemia (most important — replace potassium; combine with potassium citrate — dual benefit: reduces Ca AND increases citrate)
medicines.monitoring: Electrolytes (K+, Na+) 4-6 weeks after starting; renal function; uric acid; 24-hour urine calcium (target <200mg/day)
medicines.note: Combine with potassium citrate supplementation — prevents hypokalaemia AND increases urinary citrate (double benefit for calcium stone prevention)

medicines.name: Chlorthalidone
medicines.dosage: 25-50mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Preferred over HCTZ for kidney stone prevention in some guidelines — longer duration of action; more sustained reduction in urinary calcium

medicines.name: Indapamide
medicines.dosage: 1.5-2.5mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Thiazide-like diuretic; effective for hypercalciuria; lower metabolic side effects than HCTZ (less hypokalaemia, less hyperuricaemia); remains effective in mild CKD

categories.purpose: Form soluble disulphide complexes with cystine, dramatically increasing its solubility in urine. Reserved for cystine stone formers who continue to form stones despite adequate fluid intake and alkalinisation.

medicines.name: Tiopronin (Alpha-Mercaptopropionylglycine)
medicines.dosage: Start 300-400mg/day in 3 divided doses; titrate based on 24-hour urine cystine levels; may need up to 2000mg/day; take with large glass of water
medicines.use_case: Cystine stone prevention when high fluid intake and alkalinisation alone insufficient; PREFERRED over D-penicillamine (fewer severe side effects)
medicines.mechanism: Thiol group undergoes disulphide exchange with cystine → forms tiopronin-cysteine mixed disulphide (much more soluble than cystine)
medicines.monitoring: 24-hour urine cystine levels (target <250mg/day); urinalysis for proteinuria; FBC; LFTs

medicines.name: D-Penicillamine
medicines.dosage: 250mg initially; increase to 1000-1500mg/day in divided doses; always with pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) 50mg/day to prevent deficiency
medicines.use_case: Cystine stone prevention; effective but significant side effect profile — now second-line after tiopronin; still used when tiopronin unavailable
side_effects: Significant side effects: nephrotic syndrome (serious), pemphigus and skin reactions, Goodpasture syndrome (rare), myasthenia gravis, SLE-like reaction, bone marrow suppression, taste disturbance, pyridoxine deficiency
medicines.monitoring: Regular FBC, urinalysis, LFTs, anti-nuclear antibody

medicines.name: Captopril
medicines.dosage: 25-75mg twice to three times daily
medicines.use_case: Third-line option for cystine stones — ACE inhibitor with free thiol group that can form captopril-cysteine mixed disulphide; much more modest reduction in cystine than tiopronin/D-penicillamine; useful as additional agent

categories.category_name: Struvite Stone Prevention — Acetohydroxamic Acid (Urease Inhibitor)
categories.purpose: Inhibit bacterial urease — the enzyme responsible for the alkaline urine that causes struvite stone formation. Used as adjunct to antibiotic therapy and surgical stone removal.

medicines.name: Acetohydroxamic Acid (AHA)
medicines.dosage: 250mg three to four times daily with meals (max 1500mg/day)
medicines.use_case: Adjunct treatment for struvite (infection) stones to inhibit urease and prevent further stone growth; used when surgery cannot completely clear stone burden
medicines.mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits bacterial urease (but NOT mammalian urease); prevents ammonia production from urea → prevents alkalinisation of urine → prevents struvite crystal formation
side_effects: Significant toxicity limits use: haemolytic anaemia (most common — Coombs negative), thrombocytopenia, deep vein thrombosis, headache, tremor, GI disturbances, teratogenic
medicines.note: High side effect profile limits use; many urologists prefer complete surgical stone removal + prolonged antibiotic therapy over chronic AHA; used primarily when complete stone removal not achievable

categories.category_name: Antibiotics — Struvite Stone Treatment and Prevention
categories.purpose: Eradicate urease-producing bacteria that cause struvite (infection) stones. Antibiotic therapy is mandatory for all struvite stones. Guided by urine culture and sensitivity.

medicines.name: Culture-Guided Antibiotics for Struvite Stones
medicines.form: Oral or IV depending on severity
medicines.dosage: Based on culture and sensitivity; typical agents: co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin-clavulanate) 625mg twice daily; trimethoprim 200mg twice daily; ciprofloxacin 500mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: Long-term antibiotic suppression after surgical clearance of struvite stones (prevent recurrence); treatment of concurrent UTI in any stone patient (critical before any stone intervention); pre-operative sterilisation of urine
medicines.duration: Varies: 1-2 weeks pre-operatively; 4-6 weeks post-PCNL; long-term low-dose suppression if complete clearance not achieved
medicines.note: Urine culture MANDATORY before any stone procedure — never operate on infected urine without pre-operative antibiotic sterilisation

categories.category_name: Procedural / Surgical Interventions for Kidney Stones
categories.purpose: Active removal of stones too large to pass spontaneously, causing persistent symptoms, complications, or in special situations (single kidney, bilateral obstruction, infection). Selection depends on stone size, location, composition, patient anatomy, and preference.

medicines.name: Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL)
medicines.description: High-energy shock waves focused onto the stone from outside the body — delivered through the skin and soft tissues — cause stone fragmentation. Fragments pass spontaneously in urine over days to weeks. Most stones require 1-3 sessions.
medicines.use_case: Renal stones 5-20mm (best results 5-15mm); upper ureteric stones; stones not suitable for or not responding to conservative management. FIRST-LINE for uncomplicated renal and upper ureteral stones in many centres.
medicines.contraindications: Pregnancy (absolute); bleeding disorders / anticoagulation; active UTI; pacemaker (relative); aortic aneurysm (nearby stone); morbid obesity (penetration limitation); skeletal deformities (targeting difficulty); stones in the distal ureter (suboptimal targeting)
medicines.stone_characteristics_for_best_results: Calcium oxalate monohydrate responds moderately; calcium oxalate dihydrate responds best; brushite (calcium hydrogen phosphate) responds poorly (very hard); cystine responds poorly; uric acid responds very well but usually chemolysis is preferred
medicines.success_rate: Stone-free rate: 70-90% for small renal stones; 75-85% for upper ureteric stones; dependent on stone size, composition, and density
complications: Temporary ureteral stent may be placed pre-procedure for large stones

medicines.name: Flexible Ureteroscopy (FURS) with Laser Lithotripsy
medicines.form: Minimally invasive endoscopic procedure under general/spinal anaesthesia
medicines.description: A flexible fiberoptic or digital ureteroscope is passed up through the urethra, bladder, and ureter to the stone. Holmium:YAG laser (or thulium fibre laser) fragments the stone into dust or small retrievable fragments. Stone fragments retrieved with a nitinol basket or allowed to pass.
medicines.use_case: Ureteric stones (all sizes and locations); renal stones <20mm; stones in lower pole calyx; failed ESWL; hard stones (cystine, brushite); obesity (ESWL has reduced penetration); pacemakers; single kidney; anticoagulated patients (can be performed); patients who cannot have ESWL
medicines.success_rate: Stone-free rate: >90% for ureteric stones; 80-95% for renal stones <20mm
complications: Need for post-procedure JJ stent (2-4 weeks)
medicines.advantages: High stone-free rate; can target all stone locations; simultaneous tissue biopsy; immediate stone analysis possible; no radiation to patient during procedure

medicines.name: Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy (PCNL)
medicines.form: Minimally invasive surgical procedure under general anaesthesia
medicines.description: A 1cm track is created from the skin surface directly into the kidney collecting system under fluoroscopic/ultrasound guidance. A nephroscope is passed through this track to the stone, which is fragmented with ultrasonic, pneumatic, or laser energy, then removed through the sheath.
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE for large renal stones >20mm; staghorn calculi; multiple renal stones; lower pole stones >15mm; stones resistant to ESWL; complex anatomical situations (horseshoe kidney, PUJ obstruction); failed ESWL or URS
medicines.success_rate: Stone-free rate: 85-95% for most renal stones; multiple sessions for staghorn calculi
complications: Bleeding (most significant — nephrostomy tract; blood transfusion in 5-15%; angioembolisation occasionally needed)
Fever and urosepsis (pre-operative urine sterilisation mandatory)
Adjacent organ injury (pleura — pleural effusion/pneumothorax with upper pole access; colon — rare)
Residual fragments (requiring second procedure or ESWL)
medicines.mini_pcnl: Mini-PCNL and Ultra-mini PCNL: smaller access tracts (12-16 Fr instead of 24-30 Fr standard) — reduced bleeding; comparable stone-free rates; growing adoption

medicines.name: Retrograde Intrarenal Surgery (RIRS)
medicines.form: Flexible ureteroscopy into the kidney — same as FURS above but specifically for intra-renal stones
medicines.use_case: Renal stones <20mm as alternative to PCNL and ESWL; particularly useful for stones <15mm in all renal locations
medicines.note: Increasing preference for FURS/RIRS over ESWL due to higher single-session stone-free rates

medicines.name: Ureteral Stenting (Double-J / JJ Stent)
medicines.form: Endoscopic procedure — placement of soft polymer stent from kidney to bladder
medicines.dosage: Stent replaced every 3-6 months; temporary use
medicines.use_case: Drainage of obstructed kidney as temporising measure before definitive stone treatment; after ureteroscopy (post-procedure drainage); pregnancy-related ureteral stone (stent until delivery); single kidney stone obstruction
complications: Stent encrustation if left too long
medicines.note: JJ stents DO NOT remove the stone — they bypass obstruction to protect the kidney while awaiting definitive treatment

medicines.name: Nephrostomy Tube (Percutaneous Nephrostomy — PCN)
medicines.form: Interventional radiology procedure — ultrasound-guided drainage tube placed through skin into kidney
medicines.use_case: Emergency relief of obstructed infected kidney (urosepsis) when immediate ureteroscopic stenting not possible; drainage while patient stabilised from urosepsis before definitive stone treatment
medicines.note: Preferred over JJ stenting in severely septic patients (can be done under ultrasound alone, no need for fluoroscopy or urologist)

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet is the cornerstone of kidney stone prevention — dietary modifications are the first and most important intervention. The most important universal measure is increasing fluid intake to achieve urine volume >2.0-2.5L/day. Additional dietary modifications depend on stone type and metabolic profile from 24-hour urine analysis. The landmark DASH diet (rich in fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy, and restricted in sodium and animal protein) has been shown to reduce kidney stone risk by 40-45% — superior to a standard low-oxalate diet.
diet_and_nutrition.most_important_dietary_rule: DRINK MORE FLUIDS — Increasing daily fluid intake to achieve urine output >2.0-2.5L/day is the single most effective dietary intervention for all stone types. This dilutes all stone-forming substances simultaneously and is safe for everyone.

recommended_foods.evidence: Very strong — every meta-analysis confirms hydration as the most important preventive measure for all stone types

items.benefit: Dilutes all stone-forming substances; increases urine volume; the most important intervention of all. Target: urine output >2.0-2.5L/day, requiring fluid intake of 2.5-3.5L/day depending on climate, activity level, and sweating.
items.target: Drink enough to make urine pale yellow/straw-coloured throughout the day; dark urine = drink more
items.frequency: Continuously throughout the day; do not wait to feel thirsty; drink before bed and after waking at night

items.food: Lemon juice and lemonade (unsweetened or low-sugar)
items.benefit: Citrate — the most important natural stone inhibitor. Lemon juice has the highest citrate content of any natural food/drink. Citrus citrate directly chelates urinary calcium and inhibits crystal formation. Clinical studies: lemonade therapy (4 oz lemon juice + 2L water daily) is an effective alternative to potassium citrate for mild hypocitraturia.
items.clinical_evidence: Barcelo et al. study: 4 oz freshly squeezed lemon juice in 2L water daily increased urinary citrate to comparable levels as potassium citrate supplementation
items.frequency: Daily — glass of freshly squeezed lemon in water morning and evening; dilute well (avoid undiluted — dental erosion)

items.benefit: High citrate content comparable to lemon; potassium; Vitamin C (moderate amounts — <1g/day); reduces stone recurrence in clinical studies. Increases urinary citrate AND pH.
items.note: Do NOT supplement with large-dose Vitamin C tablets (>1g/day) — Vitamin C metabolises to oxalate and INCREASES stone risk

items.benefit: Excellent Indian source of citrate — equivalent to lemon; available year-round; can be mixed with water without added sugar for stone prevention
items.frequency: Juice of 1-2 limes in water 2 times daily

items.benefit: High potassium; magnesium; natural citrate; low sodium; alkalinising effect beneficial for uric acid stone prevention; excellent hydration fluid with electrolytes

items.food: Herbal teas (non-caffeine: ginger, chamomile, mint, hibiscus)
items.benefit: Contributes to fluid intake without calcium oxalate (unlike regular tea which has high oxalate); hibiscus has uricosuric properties (promotes uric acid excretion); hydration without caffeine
items.note: Regular black tea and green tea are HIGH in oxalate — stone formers should moderate intake; herbal (non-tea plant) infusions are preferable

recommended_foods.category: Calcium-Rich Foods (Counterintuitively Protective — Eat Normal Amounts)
recommended_foods.evidence: Strong clinical paradox — dietary calcium REDUCES stone risk, while supplemental calcium MAY increase risk. Higher dietary calcium intake binds intestinal oxalate, preventing its absorption and reducing urinary oxalate.

items.food: Low-fat dairy: Skimmed milk, Low-fat yogurt, Low-fat curd
items.benefit: Calcium binds dietary oxalate in the gut, forming insoluble calcium oxalate that is excreted in stool rather than absorbed into urine. Higher dairy intake associated with lower stone risk in epidemiological studies. Also provides protein without excess purines.
items.target: 1000-1200mg calcium per day from DIETARY sources (not supplements)
items.important: Calcium from dairy WITH MEALS binds oxalate at the same time — protective. Calcium supplements taken WITHOUT food do not bind oxalate and may increase urinary calcium — potentially harmful. Always take calcium supplements WITH meals.

items.benefit: Dietary calcium; protein; lower oxalate than nuts and leafy greens; paneer is excellent low-oxalate calcium source popular in Indian diet
Non-dairy calcium source; take with meals for oxalate-binding benefit

recommended_foods.category: Potassium and Citrate-Rich Fruits and Vegetables
recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — potassium-rich diet reduces urinary calcium; citrate in fruits is a stone inhibitor; DASH diet high in fruits/vegetables reduces stone risk 40%

items.food: Bananas, Oranges, Lemons, Limes, Melons, Peaches, Pears, Apples
items.benefit: High potassium reduces urinary calcium (potassium promotes renal calcium reabsorption); citrate in citrus reduces stone formation; antioxidants; fibre; low to moderate oxalate
items.note: Avoid very high doses of Vitamin C supplementation — dietary vitamin C in fruits at normal portions is safe

items.food: Cucumbers, Celery, Tomatoes, Bell peppers, Broccoli (moderate)
items.benefit: High water content contributes to hydration; potassium; low oxalate; anti-inflammatory; tomatoes contain lycopene; moderate citrate
High water content (watermelon is 92% water — natural hydration food); potassium; low oxalate; diuretic properties; cherry: anti-gout, reduces uric acid

items.food: Sweet potato (boiled/steamed, NOT with skin for high-oxalate formers)
items.benefit: Potassium; beta-carotene; magnesium; moderate oxalate (lower with boiling and discarding water)
items.frequency: Several times per week; boil in large water and discard to reduce oxalate

recommended_foods.evidence: Moderate — magnesium inhibits calcium oxalate crystal formation; magnesium forms complexes with oxalate reducing free oxalate in urine

items.food: Avocado, Banana, Brown rice, Oats, Quinoa
items.benefit: Magnesium — stone crystallisation inhibitor; forms magnesium oxalate (more soluble than calcium oxalate); potassium; fibre; anti-inflammatory

items.food: Cooked legumes: Lentils, Chickpeas, Kidney beans (boiled and rinsed)
items.benefit: Magnesium; plant protein (does not increase urinary uric acid unlike animal protein); fibre; replacing animal protein with plant protein reduces stone risk
items.note: Plant protein from legumes PREFERRED over animal protein — animal protein increases urinary calcium, oxalate, and uric acid; legumes do not have this effect despite containing moderate oxalate

recommended_foods.category: Foods Beneficial for Specific Stone Types

items.food: Low-fat animal protein (fish, chicken without skin) — in MODERATE portions
items.benefit: Protein necessary but AMOUNT matters: target 0.8-1.0g/kg body weight daily. Replace red meat with fish (lower purine, omega-3 anti-inflammatory) or plant protein where possible
items.target: Maximum 150-200g animal protein per day (about one palm-sized portion); reduce red meat specifically
items.frequency: Fish 2-3 times weekly; chicken 2-3 times weekly; minimise red meat and processed meats

items.food: Tart cherries (for uric acid stone prevention)
items.benefit: Anthocyanins reduce uric acid levels and reduce gout flares; specifically beneficial for uric acid stone formers and gout patients
items.frequency: Small glass of tart cherry juice daily or handful of fresh/dried tart cherries

items.food: Brown rice, Whole wheat, Oats (MODERATE fibre intake)
items.benefit: Phytate in whole grains is a mild stone inhibitor; fibre reduces intestinal calcium and oxalate absorption; complex carbohydrates preferred over refined

foods_to_avoid.reason: Sodium is the most important dietary stone promoter after low fluid intake. Every 100mmol of sodium excreted in urine results in approximately 25mg extra calcium in the urine (sodium and calcium share the same tubular reabsorption transport mechanism). High sodium also reduces urinary citrate and increases stone risk through multiple mechanisms.
foods_to_avoid.target: Sodium <2.3g/day (5.75g salt); ideally <2g/day for recurrent stone formers
examples: Table salt added in cooking or at the table — reduce to near-zero
Processed and packaged foods (highest hidden sodium source)
Canned foods and canned vegetables
Soy sauce, fish sauce — extremely high sodium
Papad, pickles (achaar), salty snacks — very high sodium
Restaurant food and takeaways — often very high sodium
Salted butter and cheese
foods_to_avoid.tip: Replace salt with lemon juice, herbs, and spices for flavour

foods_to_avoid.food: Animal Protein in Excess (Red Meat, Organ Meats, Poultry — Large Portions)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Excess animal protein: (1) Increases urinary calcium (protein induces bone resorption and reduces tubular calcium reabsorption); (2) Increases urinary oxalate; (3) Increases urinary uric acid (purines in meat); (4) DECREASES urinary citrate (produces metabolic acidosis); (5) Decreases urine pH (acidifies urine — promotes uric acid stones). Every 50g extra animal protein/day increases stone risk by 25%.
foods_to_avoid.target: Maximum 0.8-1.0g protein per kg body weight daily; ≤150g animal protein per day
examples: Beef, lamb, pork (red meat) — especially in large portions
Organ meats (liver, kidney — highest in purines)
Processed meats (sausages, salami, bacon)
Excessive poultry (although lower purine than red meat)
Shellfish (high purines — especially for uric acid stone formers)

foods_to_avoid.food: High-Oxalate Foods (for Calcium Oxalate Stone Formers Only)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Oxalate is the most powerful promoter of calcium oxalate supersaturation — 8 times more potent per unit increase than calcium. Dietary restriction appropriate for patients with documented hyperoxaluria (>45mg/day on 24-hour urine). Important nuance: dietary oxalate should be restricted but dietary CALCIUM should NOT be restricted (calcium in gut binds oxalate — protective).
very_high_oxalate_foods_restrict: Spinach (highest oxalate food — 800mg/100g raw) — eat in very small portions; boiling and discarding water reduces oxalate 30-50%
Regular black tea and green tea (strongly brewed — 100-200mg/cup)
Soy products (soy milk, tofu made with calcium sulfate is lower)
Sweet potato (moderate; reduce by boiling with skin off)
foods_to_avoid.note: Completely eliminating all these foods is unnecessary and unsustainable. Focus on the very highest sources. Always consume calcium-rich food (dairy) at same meal to bind any dietary oxalate.
foods_to_avoid.cooking_tip: Boiling high-oxalate vegetables and discarding the cooking water reduces oxalate content by 30-70% — effective simple strategy

foods_to_avoid.food: Purine-Rich Foods (for Uric Acid Stone and Calcium Oxalate Stone with Hyperuricosuria)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Purines are metabolised to uric acid. Dietary purines increase urinary uric acid, which promotes uric acid stone formation directly AND promotes calcium oxalate stone formation through heterogeneous nucleation. Uric acid stones form only in acid urine — combining low-purine diet with urine alkalinisation is extremely effective.
examples: Organ meats (liver, kidney, sweetbreads) — highest purine content
Sardines, anchovies, mackerel, herring, sprats — oily fish with high purines
Shellfish (oysters, shrimp, crab, lobster)
Yeast extracts (Marmite, Vegemite)
Beer (contains both alcohol AND guanosine — double purine effect; strongest gout/uric acid stone trigger)
Red meat in large portions

foods_to_avoid.reason: Alcohol causes dehydration (diuretic effect) — reduces urine volume, concentrating all stone-forming substances. Beer specifically: high in purines (guanosine) AND alcohol = strongest single dietary promoter of uric acid stones. Alcohol also raises uric acid levels by increasing urate production and reducing renal excretion.
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Minimise or eliminate alcohol, especially beer. If consumed — drink equal volume of water alongside
examples: Beer (highest risk for uric acid stones — double purine + alcohol effect)
Spirits and wine — moderate risk; dehydration effect
All alcoholic beverages

foods_to_avoid.reason: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is metabolically converted to oxalate in the body. Doses >1g/day significantly increase urinary oxalate and substantially raise calcium oxalate stone risk. DIETARY vitamin C from fruits and vegetables at normal portions is safe and beneficial.
foods_to_avoid.target: No vitamin C supplementation above 500mg/day for stone formers; dietary vitamin C from food is fine
foods_to_avoid.note: Do NOT take large vitamin C supplements — always tell your pharmacist you are a stone former

foods_to_avoid.food: Calcium Supplements — Caution (Not a Universal Avoidance)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Calcium supplements (tablets taken BETWEEN meals or on empty stomach) bypass the gut-binding mechanism and are absorbed as free calcium, increasing urinary calcium. Unlike dietary calcium, supplements without food have no opportunity to bind intestinal oxalate. Associated with 20-40% higher stone risk in supplement users.
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: ALWAYS take calcium supplements WITH meals (to bind intestinal oxalate). Prefer dietary calcium from dairy over supplements. If supplementation necessary: calcium citrate is preferable to calcium carbonate (more soluble, lower stone risk, can be taken without food).
foods_to_avoid.note: Women on calcium supplements for osteoporosis: discuss stone risk with doctor; take with food; monitor urinary calcium

foods_to_avoid.food: Refined Sugars and Fructose (Especially Sugary Beverages)
foods_to_avoid.reason: High fructose and refined sugar intake: increases urinary calcium, oxalate, and uric acid; promotes insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome → acid urine pH (uric acid stones); increases stone formation risk. Each additional daily serving of sugary drinks associated with 11-25% higher stone risk in prospective studies.
examples: Soft drinks / sodas (especially cola — high phosphoric acid too)
Sugary fruit juices
Energy drinks
Confectionery and sweets

foods_to_avoid.food: Low Fluid Intake — The Most Important Thing to Avoid
foods_to_avoid.reason: Insufficient fluid intake is the single most important avoidable cause of kidney stones. Dark yellow/amber urine at any time indicates inadequate hydration and dangerous stone-promoting conditions. Even one day of poor fluid intake significantly raises stone risk.
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: If urine is ever more yellow than pale straw colour — drink MORE immediately
foods_to_avoid.target: Pale yellow urine throughout the entire day and night; urine output >2.0-2.5L/day

sample_meal_plan.note: This general anti-stone meal plan is appropriate for most calcium oxalate stone formers. Specific modifications required based on stone type and 24-hour urine analysis results. Consult a dietitian and urologist for personalised guidance.
sample_meal_plan.wake_up: 2 large glasses of water (500mL) immediately upon waking + juice of 1 lemon or lime in water
